we have developed an efficient algorithm to compute the residual-phase on a Lefshetz thimble, which scales as $O(VN^2T^2)$, where $V$, $N$ and $T$ denote the volume, the number of stochastic estimates, and the length of the gradient-flow trajectory, respectively, and that we have tested the code and verified the scaling.
we have developed a new algorithm for the efficient computation of the residual phase on Lefschetz Thimbles.
we have proposed a new, more efficient method to compute a residual phase that appears in Monte Carlo calculations on Lefschetz throats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of numerical methods to compute observables in Quantum Field Theories (QFTs) on the so-called Lefschetz Thimbles (LTs).
the computation of the so-called residual phases in the context of the Lefschetz-thimble approach to the sign problem.
the development of a new method for computing the partition function in quantum field theory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the residual phase is a nuisance, which can be dealt with, but which does not seem to be a fundamental obstacle to performing Monte Carlo simulations on a Lefchetz thimble.
the cost of computing a Lefschatz integral on a thimble is $O(N^2 V^2)$, where $N$ and $V$ are the number of stochastic estimates and the volume of the system, respectively.
our method is a promising tool for Monte Carlo simulations on Lefschetz-thimbles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our code can be used to compute the residual phases in the presence of a first order phase transition.
the cost of the residual phase is comparable to that of a Monte Carlo simulation in the standard Euclidean path integral.
we have shown that it is possible to compute the residual phases on a Lefshetz thimble efficiently and with high precision.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for a given physical system and a given number of Monte Carlo iterations, the cost of computing a Lefschettz thimble path integral scales linearly with volume.
the residual phase can be efficiently computed in a wide range of applications.
the computation of the residual phase is not the bottleneck in Monte Carlo calculations on Lefschetz-thimbles.
